short_title: Entry into Force of an IMO Convention
text_verbatim: Discuss the procedure of entry into force of an IMO convention after its adoption? State the provision and its importance towards entry into force of the convention. For a convention of important technical nature state the general rules/conditions observed by the states for its entry into force. Explain the terms (i) Accession (ii) Signature subject to Ratification, acceptance or approval. (16)

sources: PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7, from QP2602/Q7): IMO conventions page - the treaty process. Adoption is by the relevant IMO organ or by a diplomatic conference. A State may express consent by signature alone where the treaty so provides; most multilateral treaties instead allow signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, where signature does not bind and the State must subsequently deposit a formal instrument with the depositary. The practice originated when communications were slow, protecting representatives from exceeding their authority, and States now use it to allow time to enact the necessary domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements. It cites Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties Article 14(2) for acceptance and approval and Article 15 for accession.

PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7, from QP2602/Q7): IMO conventions page - entry into force and amendment. A convention becomes binding only after governments formally accept it. Early conventions typically required acceptance by two-thirds of contracting States. Conventions of an important technical nature generally set higher requirements involving both a number of States and a percentage of world merchant fleet gross tonnage. The tacit acceptance procedure was devised to accelerate amendment: an amendment is deemed to have been accepted unless objections are received before a deadline. Amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances under the explicit procedure and none entered into force.

PRIMARY (READ IN FULL THIS SESSION): Resolution FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023, Amendments to the Annex to the Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic, 1965, read from the IMO resolutions CDN. Operative paragraph 1 adopts the amendments in accordance with article VII(2)(a). Operative paragraph 2 DETERMINES, in accordance with article VII(2)(b), that the amendments shall enter into force on 1 January 2025 unless, prior to 1 October 2024, at least one third of Contracting Governments have notified the Secretary-General in writing that they do not accept the amendments. This is the tacit acceptance procedure stated in operative text, with both dates, and it is the same procedure this question asks about.

PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7): IMO Circular Letter No.5005, 11 April 2025. The Secretary-General transmits the draft revised consolidated MARPOL Annex VI 'in accordance with article 16(2)(a) of the MARPOL Convention ... for consideration with a view to adoption at MEPC/ES.2 (14 to 17 October 2025) in accordance with articles 16(2)(b), (c) and (d) of said Convention'. This establishes which limb of MARPOL article 16 governs circulation and which governs adoption.

PRIMARY (READ THIS SESSION): IMO press briefing on the outcome of MEPC/ES.2, 14 to 17 October 2025. The IMO Net-Zero Framework was NOT adopted. The extraordinary session was adjourned and will be reconvened in twelve months' time, that is in October 2026, Member States continuing to work towards consensus in the interim. The Intersessional Working Group on GHG emissions reduction proceeded as scheduled from 20 to 24 October 2025.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7, from QP2602/Q7): convention summaries confirming the entry into force conditions actually used. SOLAS 1974 was adopted on 1 November 1974 and entered into force on 25 May 1980, its condition being acceptance by not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. The 1978 MARPOL Protocol provided for entry into force twelve months after not less than fifteen States, the combined merchant fleets of which constitute not less than fifty per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping, had become Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage.

INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED (MIW verification record QP2603/Q9): the Hong Kong Convention entered into force on 26 June 2025. Its Article 17 entry into force condition is a triple one - 24 months after ratification by 15 States, representing 40 per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage, whose combined maximum annual ship recycling volume during the preceding ten years constitutes not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage. This is the worked example of a technical-convention entry into force condition that this paper supplies in its own Q8.

blocks.h: 1. Adoption is not entry into force

blocks.p: A convention is adopted either by the competent IMO organ - the Assembly, MSC, MEPC or Legal Committee - or by a diplomatic conference. Adoption settles the text and does no more: it binds no State, and an adopted convention may never enter into force at all. The text is then opened for signature and deposited with the Secretary-General of IMO as depositary.

blocks.h: 2. How a State expresses consent to be bound

blocks.p: Between adoption and entry into force sits the step that actually matters: each State must express its consent to be bound, by one of three routes -

ul: signature alone, where the treaty so provides or the negotiating States so agreed;
signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, which is the normal course for multilateral conventions;
accession, where the State did not sign within the signature period.

blocks.p: In the second and third cases the State is bound only on depositing a formal instrument with the depositary, who records it, counts it towards the entry into force condition, and notifies all other States.

blocks.h: 3. The two terms the question names

blocks.p: (ii) Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval. The State signs, but the signature does not bind it; it indicates an intention to proceed. The State becomes a party only on later depositing an instrument of ratification. Its modern purpose is to give the State time to enact the necessary domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements before committing internationally. Acceptance and approval are the same act under less formal names, used where a constitution does not demand the fuller procedure: VCLT Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification. In legal effect the three are identical.

(i) Accession. The means by which a State becomes party to a treaty it did not sign - because the signature period has closed, or because it was not a negotiating State. It is a single step: no prior signature, simply deposit of an instrument of accession, permitted by VCLT Article 15 where the treaty so provides. Once deposited it has exactly the same legal effect as ratification. The difference is the route, not the destination.

blocks.h: 4. The entry into force provision, and why it matters

blocks.p: Every convention contains a final clause fixing entry into force, normally a threshold of acceptances plus a waiting period. Its importance is fourfold:

ul: it prevents an instrument binding a handful of States while the rest operate to another standard, which would distort competition;
it fixes a certain date from which obligations, surveys and certificates run, so Administrations, recognised organisations, owners and yards all work to one deadline;
it provides the interval in which flag States legislate, class develops rules, and industry builds or retrofits;
it gives legitimacy - a convention in force across most world tonnage can be enforced through port State control against ships of non-parties, which is what makes no more favourable treatment work.

blocks.h: 5. Conventions of an important technical nature

blocks.p: For a convention of important technical nature - one dictating construction, equipment or operation - States observe a stiffer double condition: a number of States and a percentage of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. A count of States alone could be satisfied by many small registries while the major fleets stayed outside, leaving a convention in force on paper and irrelevant at sea.

ul: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, requiring not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; in force 25 May 1980.
The 1978 MARPOL Protocol - in force twelve months after not less than fifteen States constituting not less than fifty per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage had become Parties.

blocks.p: Older conventions typically required two-thirds of contracting States, which occasionally meant more acceptances were needed to bring an instrument into force than to amend it.

This paper supplies its own worked example, and it is a good one because the condition was actually satisfied only months before this examination. The Hong Kong Convention uses a triple condition under Article 17 - 24 months after ratification by 15 States, representing 40 per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage, whose combined maximum annual ship recycling volume over the preceding ten years is not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage. The third limb is what made it so slow: it required the major recycling States to join, not merely the major fleet States. It entered into force on 26 June 2025.

blocks.h: 6. Keeping the convention current once in force

blocks.p: A technical convention is worthless if it cannot keep pace, and explicit acceptance failed on exactly that point: amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances and none entered into force.

IMO's answer was the tacit acceptance procedure, used in SOLAS 1974, MARPOL, the FAL Convention and the collision regulations. It reverses the default: an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted on a specified date unless objections are received beforehand from an agreed number of Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication to Contracting Governments, unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. Amendments now enter into force typically within 18 to 24 months.

The procedure can be quoted exactly, from an instrument that took effect earlier in the year of this examination. Resolution FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023 under FAL Convention article VII(2)(a), determines under article VII(2)(b) that the amendments shall enter into force on 1 January 2025 unless, prior to 1 October 2024, at least one third of Contracting Governments have notified the Secretary-General in writing that they do not accept them. No such objection was made and the amendments took effect on 1 January 2025. That is tacit acceptance in operative words, with both of its dates.

It is worth ending on the point the question begins with, because a case running at the date of this examination proves it. Under MARPOL article 16(2)(a) the Secretary-General circulated the draft revised Annex VI - the IMO Net-Zero Framework - on 11 April 2025, expressly for consideration with a view to adoption at an extraordinary session under article 16(2)(b), (c) and (d). That session, MEPC/ES.2, met from 14 to 17 October 2025 - one month before this paper - and adjourned for twelve months without adopting the Framework. Circulation had occurred; the adoption step had been convened and not taken. A candidate who understands this question can say precisely why that instrument bound nobody at the date of the examination.

Finally, once a convention is in force internationally each flag State must still give it domestic effect. In India at this examination that is the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it, and it is that domestic instrument which is enforced against the ship.

The stem prints no limbs but contains four separate demands and then names two terms. The route answers them in the order asked and gives the two named terms a heading of their own, because the examiner has singled them out and an answer that defines them in passing inside a general narrative will not be credited for them. Steps 6 and 7 are the pay-off: a candidate who can name tacit acceptance, quote a real determination with its dates, and then point to an adoption that did not happen has shown he understands the machinery rather than memorised it.

blocks.h: Four words that are not synonyms

blocks.p: Adoption settles the text. Signature may or may not bind, depending on what the treaty says. Ratification, acceptance, approval or accession is the act that binds the State, and it binds on deposit, not on decision at home. Entry into force is when the instrument starts to operate, for those States and thereafter for later parties. Candidates use all four as though they meant the same thing, and the whole question is built on their not meaning the same thing.

blocks.h: This paper answers its own question three times over

blocks.p: Revise this question together with two others on the same paper, because between them they supply every stage of the ladder as a real case. The Hong Kong Convention shows an entry into force condition satisfied - a triple condition, met after sixteen years, in force from 26 June 2025. The FAL amendments show tacit acceptance completed - determined in 2023, unopposed, effective 1 January 2025. And the Net-Zero Framework shows an adoption step convened and not taken, one month before this examination. Abstract machinery in the morning; three live cases on the same question paper.

blocks.h: The same problem exists in domestic law

blocks.p: An Indian Act is passed, then receives assent, then commences on a date appointed by notification - and it is not law until it commences. That is structurally the same three-stage problem as adoption, ratification and entry into force. The example current at this examination is exact: the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had received the assent of the President on 18 August 2025, three months before this paper, and had not commenced. It was brought into force only on 15 March 2026. At this sitting the operative statute was still the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 - and a candidate who wrote that the 2025 Act governed would have been wrong for exactly the reason this question is about.

blocks.h: Why tonnage and not just a headcount

blocks.p: The double condition looks like bureaucratic detail and is in fact the most commercially significant sentence in the answer. A safety convention that binds fifty small registries and none of the major fleets creates a competitive distortion rather than a safety improvement: compliant ships carry the cost and non-compliant ships take the trade. Requiring a percentage of world gross tonnage ensures the instrument binds the fleet that actually carries the cargo, which is what then makes port State control and no more favourable treatment effective against the remainder. The Hong Kong Convention goes one better and requires a percentage of world recycling capacity too, because a ship recycling convention that the recycling States had not joined would have regulated nothing.

ul: Saying a convention applies once IMO adopts it. Adoption binds nobody.
Treating accession as a lesser status. Once deposited it has identical effect to ratification.
Saying ratification is deposit with IMO of a signed convention. It is deposit of a separate formal instrument.
Giving the entry into force condition as a number of States only, and omitting the tonnage percentage, on a question that expressly asks about conventions of important technical nature.
Describing tacit acceptance as automatic amendment. It is deemed acceptance in the absence of objection by a specified proportion.
Stopping at entry into force and never mentioning that the flag State must still give domestic effect - which is what actually binds the ship.
'State the provision and its importance' - two demands. Describing the provision without saying why it matters loses half of them.
'For a convention of important technical nature' - this signals the double condition of States plus tonnage. It is the single most specific thing the question asks for.

'Explain the terms (i) Accession (ii) Signature subject to Ratification, acceptance or approval' - two terms, expressly numbered. Answer them as such, and contrast them: one is a single step, the other is two.

A currency trap in reverse: the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 is easy to reach for as the domestic instrument, and at this examination it had received assent but had not commenced. The answer is the 1958 Act.

blocks.p: Hold the spine as five words in order: ADOPT - SIGN - RATIFY - IN FORCE - AMEND. Then hang the numbers on it: SOLAS 1974 needed 25 States and 50% and took from 1974 to 1980; the 1978 MARPOL Protocol needed 15 States and 50% plus twelve months; the Hong Kong Convention needed 15 States, 40% tonnage and 3% recycling volume; tacit acceptance for SOLAS runs two years, defeated by one-third of Governments or 50% of tonnage. And remember the two named terms as a contrast: accession is one step, signature-subject-to-ratification is two.

ul: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Article 14(2) acceptance and approval; Article 15 accession.
SOLAS 1974 - entry into force condition (25 States, 50% world tonnage) and the tacit acceptance amendment procedure.
MARPOL - Article 15 entry into force; Article 16 amendments, with 16(2)(a) circulation and 16(2)(b), (c), (d) adoption; 1978 Protocol (15 States, 50%).
FAL Convention - article VII(2)(a) adoption and VII(2)(b) tacit acceptance, recited in the operative text of resolution FAL.15(47).
Hong Kong Convention - Article 17, the triple entry into force condition; in force 26 June 2025.
IMO Convention, Article 38(e) - the Organization's depositary and convention functions.
Merchant Shipping Act 1958 (India) - the operative domestic statute at this sitting.

blocks.p: The treaty-making machinery is the most stable material on this paper: it has not changed materially since tacit acceptance was introduced, so nothing in steps 1 to 6 is sitting-relative and no regression from the August 2025 donor was needed there. What did need rewriting is the live example. At the donor's sitting the Net-Zero Framework had been circulated and its adoption was still ahead; by this examination the adoption session had met and adjourned for twelve months without adopting. Copying the donor's sentence would have stated a superseded position. The limitation that remains is one of sourcing rather than currency: MIW holds no licensed copy of SOLAS, so the SOLAS provisions are cited by name and effect from IMO's own explanatory material rather than by asserted article number, and the Vienna Convention articles are cited as quoted on the IMO page. FAL article VII(2)(a) and VII(2)(b) are primary, being recited in the operative text of FAL.15(47), which was read in full.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A treaty-law procedure question. The examiner is testing whether a Chief Engineer understands why a convention he has heard of may not yet apply to his ship, and whether he can distinguish four terms of art that are routinely used as synonyms.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, printed as a single undivided question with four demands and two lettered terms carrying no separate marks. The terms are weighted as roughly a quarter of the answer because the paper singles them out.

technical_ambiguities: 'Ratification, acceptance and approval' are three names for acts of identical legal effect, distinguished only by constitutional formality. Presenting them as three different procedures is wrong; presenting them as one word is incomplete.
Accession and ratification reach the same destination by different routes. The contrast the examiner wants is one step versus two, not a difference in status.

Entry into force of the CONVENTION and entry into force of an AMENDMENT run on different machinery - threshold plus waiting period for the first, tacit acceptance for the second. Both are asked for and they must not be merged.
The Hong Kong Convention condition is often summarised as a double condition like SOLAS. It is a TRIPLE condition, and the third limb - recycling volume - is the reason it took sixteen years.

SOLAS tacit acceptance: deemed accepted after two years unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments or Governments holding not less than 50% of world gross tonnage
FAL.15(47): adopted 17 March 2023, in force 1 January 2025 unless one third of Contracting Governments objected before 1 October 2024
Older conventions commonly required two-thirds of contracting States
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The entry into force final clause of the convention concerned, read with the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties Articles 14(2) and 15; and for amendment, the tacit acceptance procedure in SOLAS 1974, MARPOL article 16 and FAL Convention article VII(2)(b).
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating adoption, signature, ratification and entry into force as one event. Adoption settles the text and binds nobody; signature ordinarily does not bind either; the State is bound only when it deposits a formal instrument; and the convention operates only when its own entry into force condition is met. The second trap is answering the technical-convention limb with a number of States and omitting the percentage of world merchant gross tonnage, which is the specific thing that limb asks for. The third is a currency trap in reverse: naming the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 as the domestic instrument. It had received assent on 18 August 2025 but did not commence until 15 March 2026, so at this sitting the operative statute was the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 - which is the very distinction this question is about.

understand_first: The point of this question is that a convention passes through several distinct stages, and at every stage it is not yet law for your ship. Adoption fixes the words. Signature usually promises nothing. Ratification or accession binds the State, and only when the instrument is physically deposited. Entry into force starts the obligations running. And even then, what is actually enforced against the ship in an Indian port is the domestic legislation giving effect to the convention. A Chief Engineer who can place an instrument on that ladder can answer 'does this apply to me?' - which is what the question is really about. This paper is unusually generous to anyone who has understood it, because it carries three live cases of the ladder at three different rungs: a condition satisfied, an amendment tacitly accepted, and an adoption convened and not taken.
memory_cue: The spine is in order: ADOPT (1) - CONSENT (2) - THE TWO TERMS (3) - IN FORCE (4) - TONNAGE TEST (5) - AMEND (6) - NOT ADOPTED (7). Numbers: SOLAS 25 and 50; MARPOL 78 fifteen and 50; Hong Kong 15, 40 and 3; tacit acceptance two years, one-third or 50 per cent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the entry into force of an IMO convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Adoption is not entry into force. 2 How a State expresses consent to be bound. 3 The two terms named - accession, and signature subject to ratification. 4 The entry into force provision and why it matters. 5 Conventions of important technical nature. 6 Keeping the convention current - tacit acceptance. 7 Adoption is not automatic either, and domestic effect.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem contains four demands and names two terms; the route answers them in that order and gives the named terms their own heading.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain the difference between accession and signature subject to ratification.
retrieval_cards.answer: Signature subject to ratification is a two-step route: the State signs, which does not bind it, and becomes a party only on later depositing an instrument of ratification - the interval giving it time to enact domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements. Accession is a single step used where the State did not sign, whether because the signature period closed or because it was not a negotiating State: it simply deposits an instrument of accession. Once deposited, both have identical legal effect.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner names both terms expressly, so they must be contrasted - one step against two - not merely defined.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are acceptance and approval, and how do they differ from ratification?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are the same act as ratification under less formal names, used where a State's constitution does not require the fuller procedure. VCLT Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification. In legal effect the three are identical.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates often present them as three different procedures. They are three names for one binding act.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What entry into force condition is used for a convention of important technical nature, and give two examples.
retrieval_cards.answer: A double condition - a minimum number of States and a minimum percentage of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. SOLAS 1974 required not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of world merchant gross tonnage; adopted 1 November 1974, in force 25 May 1980. The Hong Kong Convention went further with a triple condition under Article 17 - 24 months after 15 States, 40 per cent of world merchant gross tonnage, and a combined maximum annual recycling volume of not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage - and entered into force on 26 June 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: The tonnage percentage is the specific thing this limb asks for, and it is the half most often omitted. The Hong Kong example is on this same paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the tacit acceptance procedure and why was it introduced? Quote a real determination.
retrieval_cards.answer: An amendment to the technical annexes is deemed to have been accepted on a specified date unless objections are received beforehand from an agreed number of Parties. It was introduced because explicit acceptance had failed: amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never gathered enough acceptances and none entered into force. For SOLAS 1974 the period is two years from communication, defeated by objection from more than one-third of Contracting Governments or from Governments holding not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. Resolution FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023, states it in operative words: the amendments shall enter into force on 1 January 2025 unless, prior to 1 October 2024, at least one third of Contracting Governments notify the Secretary-General in writing that they do not accept them.
retrieval_cards.why: It reverses the default from opt-in to opt-out, which is the whole reason technical conventions can now keep pace - and FAL.15(47) lets it be quoted rather than paraphrased.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A convention has been adopted by IMO. Does it apply to your ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: No, not by adoption alone. Adoption settles the text and binds no State. The State must express consent to be bound by depositing an instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession; the convention must then satisfy its own entry into force condition; and the flag State must give it domestic effect - in India at this sitting through the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and rules made under it - before it is enforced against the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the practical question the whole topic exists to answer, and the four-stage chain is the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give an example, current at this sitting, of a draft amendment circulated for adoption where adoption did not follow.
retrieval_cards.answer: The draft revised MARPOL Annex VI containing the IMO Net-Zero Framework. It was circulated by IMO Circular Letter No.5005 of 11 April 2025 in accordance with MARPOL article 16(2)(a), for consideration with a view to adoption at the extraordinary session MEPC/ES.2 under article 16(2)(b), (c) and (d). That session met from 14 to 17 October 2025 - one month before this examination - and adjourned for twelve months without adopting the Framework, to reconvene in October 2026. Circulated, therefore, but not adopted, and binding nobody at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows that even the adoption step is not automatic, and it was one month old at the date of this examination.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statute gives domestic effect to IMO conventions at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had received the assent of the President on 18 August 2025, three months before this examination, but assent is not commencement: it was brought into force only on 15 March 2026. Naming the 2025 Act here would be wrong for precisely the reason this question exists.
retrieval_cards.why: The domestic ladder repeats the international one, and this sitting falls in the gap between assent and commencement.
